title: Employee Stock Options (ESOs): Mechanics, Vesting, Dilution, Backdating Scandals, and Hull-White Valuation
prerequisites: European and American option valuation principles
Corporate finance and equity dilution basics
learningOutcomes: Explain the non-transferable structure, vesting periods (cliff and graded), and forfeiture conditions of employee stock options ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Analyze the moral hazard of asymmetric payoffs and the corporate governance implications of executive risk aversion ([fact-03], [fact-10]).
Evaluate accounting expensing mandates (FAS 123R / ASC 718, IFRS 2) and the dilutive EPS impact of newly issued shares ([fact-04], [fact-05]).
Examine historical option backdating and spring loading scandals uncovered by Erik Lie ([fact-06]).
Apply the Hull-White binomial model incorporating early exercise multiples M and forfeiture rates lambda to correct Black-Scholes overvaluation ([fact-07], [fact-08]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: ESOs are strictly non-transferable call options granted to staff and executives; they cannot be sold, traded, or hedged, and are subject to immediate forfeiture if the employee departs prior to vesting ([fact-01]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Standard BSM significantly overvalues ESOs because employees cannot trade their stock and exercise early (at multiple M) to lock in gains and diversify, requiring specialized binomial models like Hull-White ([fact-07], [fact-08]).

misconceptions.misconception: Believing high leverage creates free profits without downside risk.
misconceptions.authorRebuttal: Unlike exchange-traded options, exercising ESOs requires the issuing corporation to issue newly minted shares of common stock, which expands the share base and dilutes future Earnings Per Share (EPS) ([fact-05]).

activeRecallQuiz.scenario: A 10-year ESO is granted at-the-money with S0 = $50.00, strike K = $50.00, risk-free rate r = 5%, volatility sigma = 30%, and zero dividends. A standard 10-year BSM European call values the option at $25.96 per share. Under the Hull-White model with a 3-year vesting period, early exercise multiple M = 1.5 (exercising at S = $75.00), and employee forfeiture rate lambda = 4% per year, the fair value drops to $18.60 per share.
activeRecallQuiz.question: 1) Why does the Hull-White binomial model value ESOs significantly lower than standard BSM? 2) What corporate impact occurs when employees exercise ESOs?
activeRecallQuiz.correctAnswer: Correctly identifying the downside risk and margin constraints.
activeRecallQuiz.explanation: Detailed pedagogical explanation grounded in source principles.

coreTakeaways: Employee stock options are non-transferable 10-year call options subject to cliff or graded vesting and forfeiture upon departure ([fact-01], [fact-02]).
Standard Black-Scholes overvalues ESOs by over 39% because executives exercise early at price multiples M to diversify undiversified human capital and wealth ([fact-07], [fact-08], [fact-10]).
ESO exercises result in newly issued shares that dilute corporate EPS, while accounting standards (FAS 123R / ASC 718) mandate grant-date fair value expensing ([fact-04], [fact-05]).
